messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame Mensah, a 72-year-old Coast Guard serviceman who had spent decades trusting routine and procedure, traced the beginning of his difficulties to a chemical exposure during a harbor response call. A storage container on the dock had ruptured, and he was among the first to move in. He remembered the strange, almost wrong stillness just before people started shouting—a pocket of silence over the water, no gulls, no machinery he could make out, only the sight of a pale vapor spreading low across the pier. He could still see it in frozen images: the sheen on the metal railing, a crewman bent over coughing, the mask on another responder not seated properly against his face. At the time he kept moving, but later the scene returned to him not as an ordinary recollection but like a film that restarted without his permission, or as sharp photographic flashes that left him shaken.

In the weeks afterward, Kwame found that when the memory came back, it hit with so much force that he had to stop whatever he was doing. He would be standing in his kitchen or checking equipment at work and suddenly feel flooded by the same dread and bodily jolt, as if he were back on the dock. Those returns of the scene convinced him that he was no longer able to handle strain the way he once had. He had come to believe that if he let himself think about the exposure at all, he would be overwhelmed beyond control. The more vividly the event replayed, the more certain he became that even a slight upset could undo him and that the world itself was fundamentally unsafe.

That shift in what he believed about himself and the world fed directly into how he moved through ordinary life. Because he was convinced danger could emerge without warning and that he would not cope if it did, he stayed on guard even at home, scanning for signs that something was off. What frightened him most was silence. A quiet room, the television turned off, the pause before his wife answered from another room—these moments felt loaded, like the breathless stillness on the dock before the seriousness of the leak became clear. He would feel his chest tighten and his body surge into readiness, as though unusual silence itself meant something harmful was about to happen.

The same thing happened on duty. In the Coast Guard station, if a corridor went unexpectedly quiet or the usual hum of radios dropped out, Kwame’s body reacted before he could think. He would feel his heart pound, his hands tense, and the dock scene would begin to unspool again in his mind. A moment of silence could call up the visual fragments so vividly that he had to step away. In that sense the memories and the sense of threat had become tightly bound: the mental replay made him feel endangered in the present, and feeling endangered made the images return with even greater force.

Over months, he tried to manage this by keeping his mind away from the exposure. He avoided dwelling on that day because he was certain that if he let the memory in, he would not be able to handle what followed. Yet the constant watchfulness seemed to trap him with the event rather than distance him from it. When he sat at home alert to every pause in the house, or when his body reacted to a sudden hush at work, he found himself right back with those photographic snapshots of vapor on the pier and men struggling to breathe. Each episode left him more persuaded that his reactions were proof of diminished resilience. He would tell himself that if a quiet room could unravel him, then he truly could not cope with even minor stress.

His marriage had narrowed around this pattern. Even inside his own home, he rarely relaxed, and his wife had begun keeping noise on in the background because she could see how quickly silence changed him. At work, he still reported for duty, but he positioned himself where activity was constant and found excuses to avoid quieter areas near the docks. These habits made sense to him because he believed the world was dangerous and that staying alert was the only thing preventing another catastrophe, but they also kept his body primed and his mind close to the worst moments of the exposure.

Kwame finally agreed to seek help after an episode at home when the house fell completely quiet during a brief power outage. The silence brought an immediate rush of heat, a pounding heart, and the full visual replay of the dock, so overwhelming that he had to sit down and could not speak for several minutes. What frightened him most was not only the memory itself but the conclusion he drew from it: that he was becoming unable to manage ordinary life, even in his own home. He came in hoping for some way to stop living as if danger were always about to break through the next silent moment.
